chapter.name: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society

questions.q:
A school's debate club prints a handout on 'Our courts' and the teacher asks the class to test it against the chapter.
Line 1: 'Societies expect fair treatment for everyone, and the government's way of ensuring justice is by framing laws.'
Line 2: 'Once a law is framed, the legislature checks that the executive follows it, so the judiciary has no watch-keeping role.'
Line 3: 'Disagreements are often settled through dialogue, mediation or adjudication by courts of law.'
(a) Which line contradicts the chapter?
(b) Rewrite that line correctly, naming both watch-keeping roles of the judiciary.
(c) Line 3 lists ways of settling disagreements. What reason does the chapter give for why disagreements and disputes arise at all?
(d) The chapter gives a reason why the judiciary must be independent of the legislature and the executive. Which of the three lines, even after correction, states that reason?
questions.a: (a) Line 2. (b) Corrected: once a law is framed, the judiciary ensures that the laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution and that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution. (c) Society has many complex interactions happening all the time, both personal and professional, so disagreements and disputes may arise from diverse contexts and situations. (d) None of the three: the chapter's reason is that an independent judiciary is essential to ensure that disputes between parties are decided in a fair and just manner, and no line says so.
s: Line 2 is the contradicting line
Both roles: laws within the Constitution; executive within its role
Many complex personal and professional interactions give rise to disputes
None of the three lines states the reason: independence ensures fair and just decisions

questions.q: A State's Revenue Department orders a farmer's well sealed. The farmer's lawyer argues that the Constitution gives the department no such power, and asks the court to say so. Assume the lawyer is right. Which of the judiciary's roles does the farmer want the court to perform?
questions.a: Ensuring that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution
o: Ensuring that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution
Ensuring that the laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution
Framing a fresh rule on wells so that the department can apply it in future
Enforcing the department's order with force, as the government is empowered to do

questions.q: A judge hears two neighbours and decides their quarrel. The chapter's phrase for this role of the judiciary is fair ___ of disputes in accordance with the law (the missing word begins with 'ad' and names the court's way of deciding a dispute, as opposed to mediation).
questions.a: adjudication

questions.q: A tailor and a client quarrel over payment. (a) Which of the chapter's three routes needs nothing more than the two of them talking? (b) If the matter is put before a court instead, which route is it, and what does the chapter say the judiciary then ensures?
questions.a: (a) Dialogue. (b) Adjudication by courts of law; the judiciary ensures fair adjudication of the dispute in accordance with the law and that everyone is treated justly and with fairness.
s: Part (a): dialogue
Part (b): adjudication; fair adjudication according to law, everyone treated justly and fairly

questions.q: Meena argues: 'We do not need a government to make people fair to each other; goodwill is enough.' Which part of the chapter's account of how governance began answers her best?
questions.a: The task of fair treatment was handed to a government, with the power to make and enforce laws, by force if needed
o: The task of fair treatment was handed to a government, with the power to make and enforce laws, by force if needed
Governance began only after the judiciary had been set up as the first pillar of government
Societies expect fair treatment, and individuals settle every dispute by talking among themselves
The Preamble was written first, and governments were formed afterwards to read it aloud

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's scheme, the judiciary is independent from the legislature and the executive.
Reason (R): An independent judiciary is essential to ensure that disputes between parties are decided in a fair and just manner.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'The judiciary has to be independent of the legislature and the executive.' (a) State the two watch-keeping roles the chapter gives the judiciary. (b) For each role, say whose conduct the judiciary is checking and why a judiciary controlled by that same body could not check it fairly. (c) Say what the chapter says an independent judiciary is essential to ensure.
questions.a: (a) It ensures that the laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution, and that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution. (b) In the first role it checks the legislature's laws; a court controlled by the legislature would be judging its own controller's work. In the second it checks the executive; a court controlled by the executive would have to rule against its own controller. (c) That disputes between parties are decided in a fair and just manner. Accept any sound reason for part (b); the chapter itself states only that an independent judiciary is essential for fair and just decisions.
s: Role 1 named
Role 2 named
Role 1: whose work is checked, and why control defeats the check
Role 2: whose conduct is checked, and why control defeats the check
Independence ensures disputes are decided in a fair and just manner

questions.q: A ministry employee's cousin is in a land dispute with a villager, and the case comes before a judge. Which arrangement fits the chapter's reasoning about the judiciary?
questions.a: The judge decides on the law, independent of the legislature and executive, so the dispute is decided fairly and justly
o: The judge decides on the law, independent of the legislature and executive, so the dispute is decided fairly and justly
The judge first asks the minister's office what outcome it prefers, as the executive runs the State and knows the parties
The judge waits for the legislature to pass a special rule for this one dispute before deciding it at all
The judge hands the case to the minister, because the executive is the pillar that settles disputes between citizens

questions.q: Imran claims: 'The government's way of ensuring justice is by framing laws, so once laws are framed the judiciary has nothing more to do.' Test each half and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right: the chapter says the government's way to ensure that justice is achieved is the framing of laws. The second half is wrong: the judiciary still has two watch-keeping roles, ensuring that the legislature's laws are within the framework of the Constitution and that the executive does not overstep its role.
s: First half supported: framing laws is the government's way
Second half wrong: the two continuing roles of the judiciary
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: A teacher asks whether a quarrel between two traders that ends through a neutral mediator, with no court judgment, counts as resolved in the chapter's sense. True or False? 'Yes: mediation is one of the routes the chapter names for resolving disputes.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says disputes between parties are often resolved through dialogue, mediation, or adjudication by courts of law, so a mediated settlement is a resolution without a judgment.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: dialogue, mediation or adjudication are all named routes

questions.q: A notice at a school fair reads: 'The judiciary is the second pillar of government and takes its orders from the executive. It settles disputes only by talking.' Correct the two errors using the chapter.
questions.a: First, the judiciary is one of three pillars and is independent from the legislature and the executive; it does not take orders from the executive. Second, disputes are resolved through dialogue, mediation or adjudication by courts of law, not only by talking.
s: Correction 1: independent of legislature and executive
Correction 2: three routes including adjudication by courts

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the chapter's idea in Column B that it illustrates.
Column A: 1. A hawker is humiliated by a local official and told she is not equal to the other traders.  2. Two firms disagree over a delivery, and the dispute is traced to their business dealings.  3. A State's new rule is challenged as outside the Constitution.  4. A government draws up rules for traffic and enforces them with fines.
Column B: a. Disputes arise from personal and professional interactions  b. Justice ensures equality and dignity  c. The judiciary keeps laws within the framework of the Constitution  d. The government's way of ensuring justice is framing laws

Write two separate one-line situations: one in which the judiciary acts in its watch-keeping role over the legislature, and one in which it acts in its role over the executive. Label which part of the chapter each situation shows.
questions.a: Sample: (1) 'A new State Act is challenged because it conflicts with the Constitution, and the court examines whether it is within the Constitution's framework' shows the role of ensuring that laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution. (2) 'A municipal office seals a shop under a power the Constitution does not give it, and the shopkeeper asks the court to rule' shows the role of ensuring that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution.
s: A situation involving a law passed by the legislature
A situation involving an executive action
Each labelled with the correct role

questions.q: At a school function a speaker says: 'The Preamble already promises social, economic and political justice, so courts add nothing.' Which line of the chapter shows what the speaker overlooks?
questions.a: The judiciary ensures fair adjudication and just treatment of everyone
o: The judiciary ensures fair adjudication and just treatment of everyone
The Preamble was drafted so that disputes need never be placed before any institution of the State
The founders of independent India left justice to the government's framing of laws alone, with no courts
Justice ensures equality and dignity only for those who vote in the elections held in the country

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say justice ensures for individuals in a society? (b) A tea-stall owner is repeatedly refused payment by a customer and no authority will hear her. Using (a), say what she is denied and what the chapter says is at stake for society.
questions.a: (a) Justice ensures that individuals can live with equality and dignity. (b) She is denied equality and dignity; the chapter says justice is essential for maintaining peace and harmony in any society, so peace and harmony are at stake.
s: Part (a): equality and dignity
Part (b): she is denied these; peace and harmony at stake

questions.q:
In a port town, a co-operative of fish-sellers finds its market stalls cancelled by a municipal office, with no one listening to its side. The members first talk to the officer. When that fails, a retired teacher both sides respect tries to help them reach a settlement but cannot make any decision for them. Finally the co-operative goes to court, which is not controlled by the municipal office.
(a) Name the three routes the co-operative has used, in order.
(b) Suppose the municipal office had no power under the Constitution to cancel the stalls. Which role of the judiciary would be at work?
(c) The chapter calls justice essential for peace and harmony. Which two things does it say justice ensures for the fish-sellers as individuals?
(d) Why does it matter to the co-operative that the court is not controlled by the municipal office?
questions.a: (a) Dialogue, mediation, adjudication by a court of law. (b) Ensuring that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution. (c) Equality and dignity. (d) Because an independent judiciary is essential to ensure that the dispute is decided in a fair and just manner; a court controlled by the office would be deciding a dispute about its own order.
s: Three routes in order
Executive not overstepping its role
Equality and dignity
Independence ensures a fair and just decision

questions.q:
Read the statements about the opening of the chapter.
1. The Preamble promises all Indian citizens social, economic and political justice.
2. The judiciary is one of the three pillars of government and is independent from the legislature and the executive.
3. The chapter says disputes between parties are resolved only by adjudication in courts of law.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Distinguish the judiciary's two watch-keeping roles in the chapter, and for each give one example of your own of what it would look at.
questions.a: Role 1: ensuring that laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution; for example a law passed by a State legislature that is challenged as contrary to it. Role 2: ensuring that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution; for example an official's order that goes beyond the powers given to the executive.
s: Role 1 stated with an example about a law of the legislature
Role 2 stated with an example about an executive action

questions.q: A Class 8 student is asked: 'Why does a democratic society need a judiciary?' Using the chapter, write a five-point answer that moves from the Preamble to the judiciary's place among the pillars of government.
questions.a: (1) The Preamble promises all citizens social, economic and political justice, and the founders laid the foundation for a sound judicial system in a democratic society. (2) Justice is essential for peace and harmony because it ensures individuals can live with equality and dignity. (3) The judiciary is the institution that ensures fair adjudication of disputes in accordance with the law and that everyone is treated justly and with fairness. (4) It is one of three pillars of government, independent from the legislature and the executive, so disputes are decided fairly. (5) It ensures that the legislature's laws are within the Constitution and that the executive does not overstep its role.
s: Preamble promise and the founders' foundation
Justice, peace, harmony, equality and dignity
Judiciary defined: fair adjudication according to law
One of three pillars, independent
The two watch-keeping roles

questions.q: The chapter says the government may enforce laws with force if needed, and also that the judiciary is independent of the executive. In three points, explain why the chapter's picture needs both.
questions.a: (1) The government has the power to administer society through laws and to enforce them, with force if needed. (2) The judiciary ensures that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution, so the power to enforce is itself kept within the Constitution. (3) For that check, and for deciding disputes fairly, the judiciary must be independent from the legislature and the executive.
s: Government's power to make and enforce laws, with force if needed
The judiciary checks that the executive does not overstep its role
Independence is essential for fair and just decisions

questions.q: Two students watch a mock trial. Rhea asks only: 'Is the final decision fair, just and reasonable?' Tarun asks only: 'Did every person involved get a full opportunity of hearing before the decision?' Which pairing matches the chapter?
questions.a: Rhea is testing substantive justice (the outcome); Tarun is testing procedural justice (the hearing)
o: Rhea is testing substantive justice (the outcome); Tarun is testing procedural justice (the hearing)
Rhea is testing procedural justice; Tarun is testing substantive justice
Both are testing substantive justice, since both concern the court's final decision
Rhea is testing the judicial system; Tarun is testing the repeal of unjust laws

questions.q:
Two imaginary courts decide the same wage dispute between a mill worker and her employer. Assume the agreed wage of Rs 9,000 a month is a fair and reasonable amount.
Court P hears the worker and the employer in full, but orders the employer to pay only Rs 2,000 a month.
Court Q orders Rs 9,000 a month, but passes the order without allowing the employer to say anything.
(a) Which court's decision fails the test of substantive justice, and why?
(b) Which court's decision fails the test of procedural justice, and why?
(c) The employer's lawyer says: 'Court Q's result is right, so nothing was wrong.' Which part of the chapter's account of procedural justice shows the flaw in this?
(d) Court Q rehears the case, lets the employer speak, and then cuts the wage to Rs 3,000. Which aspect of justice is now met and which now fails?
questions.a: (a) Court P: its outcome, Rs 2,000 against a fair Rs 9,000, is not fair, just and reasonable. (b) Court Q: the employer did not get a full opportunity of hearing before the decision. (c) Procedural justice means every person involved gets a full opportunity of hearing before the court decides, whatever the result. (d) Procedural justice is now met (the employer was heard), but substantive justice fails, since Rs 3,000 is not the fair and reasonable amount.
s: Court P fails substantive justice: outcome unreasonable
Court Q fails procedural justice: no hearing for the employer
Procedural justice needs a full hearing before the decision, whatever the result
After rehearing: procedural met, substantive fails

questions.q: A quiz asks for the colonial law, repealed after independence, that labelled certain communities as criminals by birth. It is the Criminal Tribes Act of ___.

Read the statements about law and justice.
1. The chapter says the only consequence a law can impose for not following it is imprisonment.
2. The chapter says over 1500 colonial-era laws enacted during British Rule have been repealed.
3. The chapter says the apartheid-era laws of South Africa were repealed in 1991.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Nisha claims: 'Because the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 and the Vernacular Press Act, 1878 have been repealed, the chapter says every law made during British Rule was discriminatory.' Test the claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No, the claim goes beyond the chapter. It says hundreds of colonial-era laws were found to be discriminatory and contrary to the principles of a democratic polity, and that over 1500 such laws have been repealed after the government reviewed them; the two Acts are only examples. It does not say every law of British Rule was discriminatory.
s: Chapter: hundreds of colonial laws found discriminatory, over 1500 repealed
The two Acts are examples only
Verdict: No, 'every law' is not said

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter treats a rule as just simply because the government made it.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter shows that governments have made unjust laws: over 1500 colonial laws were repealed as discriminatory, and the Jim Crow and apartheid laws are given as unjust laws elsewhere.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: repealed colonial laws and the Jim Crow and apartheid laws were unjust

questions.q: A shopkeeper who breaks a market rule is told to pay Rs 500 and to compensate a customer for a damaged item. Which two of the chapter's named consequences of breaking a law are these?
questions.a: A fine and compensation to the affected party
o: A fine and compensation to the affected party
A fine and imprisonment in some cases
Compensation to the affected party and imprisonment
Imprisonment alone, in some cases, with no payment

questions.q: In an imaginary case, a court sends a man to jail after hearing only the complainant's evidence. A later review finds that the outcome happens to be fair and reasonable. (a) State what substantive justice asks. (b) State what procedural justice means and the rule that goes with it. (c) Which aspect did the court fail, and which did it meet? (d) Explain why the chapter lists both aspects rather than one.
questions.a: (a) Substantive justice focuses on the final result and asks whether the decision is actually fair, just and reasonable. (b) Procedural justice means every person involved gets a full opportunity of hearing before the court decides; as a rule every person is presumed innocent till proved guilty. (c) It failed procedural justice, since the man was not heard, and the outcome met substantive justice. (d) A decision can be right in outcome yet unfair in how it was reached, so justice is judged on both.
s: Substantive justice stated
Procedural justice stated
The presumption of innocence rule
Failed procedural, met substantive
Both aspects are needed: outcome and way of reaching it

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say laws are? (b) Give one rule from your school and the consequence it imposes, and say which of the chapter's three named consequences it is closest to.
questions.a: (a) Laws are general rules made by the government to regulate individuals' activities in a society and to impose consequences for not following them. (b) Sample: a rule against damaging library books, with the consequence that the student pays for a new copy; it is closest to giving compensation to the affected party.
s: Part (a): general rules by the government to regulate activities, with consequences
Part (b): a valid example matched to fine, compensation or imprisonment

questions.q:
Match each imaginary law in Column A with the chapter's example it most resembles in Column B.
Column A: 1. A law requires everyone born into one community to report to the police daily.  2. A law lets officials restrict what newspapers may print.  3. A law keeps pools and restaurants for one group of people and shuts others out because of colour.  4. A law divides the whole population by race and places severe restrictions on coloured people.
Column B: a. Apartheid-era laws of South Africa  b. Criminal Tribes Act, 1871  c. Jim Crow laws  d. Vernacular Press Act, 1878

Show that, by the chapter's own account, a court could not call a verdict procedurally just if the accused was punished before being allowed to give her side, however fair the verdict later seemed. Give three points.
questions.a: (1) Procedural justice means every person involved gets a full opportunity of hearing before a decision is taken by the court. (2) The rule is that every person is presumed innocent till proved guilty, which punishment before a hearing breaks. (3) Fairness of the final result is the separate test of substantive justice, so a fair-looking verdict cannot make up for a missing hearing.
s: Full opportunity of hearing before the decision
Presumption of innocence till proved guilty
Outcome is a different aspect, substantive justice

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A court that decides after hearing only one side has failed procedural justice, even if its result is fair.
Reason (R): Substantive justice focuses on the final result or outcome of the case.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Asha says: 'The judicial system lets a person complain of a grievance and place her point of view.' Bela says: 'The judicial system makes the laws.' (a) Whose description matches the chapter? (b) According to the chapter, whose way of ensuring justice is the framing of laws?
questions.a: (a) Asha's: the judicial system enables individuals to complain in case of a grievance and to place their point of view, so that justice is ensured within the framework of the law and the Constitution. (b) The government's.
s: Part (a): Asha's, with the chapter's definition
Part (b): the government's way is framing laws

questions.q: A student concludes: 'Colonial laws were repealed only because they were old.' Which reasoning from the chapter shows what is missing?
questions.a: They were found discriminatory, contrary to democratic principles, and inconsistent with justice and the republic
o: They were found discriminatory, contrary to democratic principles, and inconsistent with justice and the republic
They were repealed because Britain asked India to review each of them as soon as British rule had come to an end in the country
They were repealed because courts had stopped hearing cases under them after the Constitution took effect
They were repealed because each of them had punished those who broke it with imprisonment alone

questions.q: (a) Give one thing the Jim Crow laws and the apartheid-era laws had in common according to the chapter. (b) Give one difference between them in country and in the date of repeal.
questions.a: (a) Both divided or restricted people on the basis of race or colour and so kept them from public facilities and a life with dignity. (b) Jim Crow laws were in parts of the United States and were officially repealed in the 1960s; the apartheid laws were in South Africa and were repealed in 1991.
s: Part (a): race or colour restrictions limiting public facilities and dignity
Part (b): United States, 1960s against South Africa, 1991

questions.q: Dev reads that during the apartheid era in South Africa people were divided by law on the basis of race, and says: 'Jim Crow laws were repealed at the same time, in 1991.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: Jim Crow laws were in parts of the United States and were officially repealed in the 1960s
o: Jim Crow laws were in parts of the United States and were officially repealed in the 1960s
Jim Crow laws were in South Africa and were repealed in the 1960s
Jim Crow laws were in India and were repealed with the Criminal Tribes Act
Jim Crow laws were in the United States and were repealed in 1991, with apartheid

questions.q: The chapter gives a rule of procedural justice that every person is presumed innocent till proved guilty. (a) State what the rule requires of a court before punishing anyone. (b) Using it, explain why a law that labelled whole communities as criminals by birth, like the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871, sits badly with the chapter's idea of justice.
questions.a: (a) A court must treat each person as innocent until she is proved guilty, after giving her a full opportunity of hearing. (b) Labelling a whole community as criminals by birth treats people as guilty without any proof against them, which cannot be reconciled with the presumption of innocence; the chapter calls such laws inconsistent with the values and principles of justice.
s: Part (a): presumed innocent till proved guilty, after a full hearing
Part (b): guilt assumed by birth, with no proof, contrary to the rule

questions.q:
An imaginary State (figures and names illustrative) passes a rule: 'No person born in the Kori community may use the town library or the public water tank, and every such person must report to the police post each week.'
(a) Which repealed law of the chapter does the labelling by birth resemble?
(b) Which foreign laws of the chapter does the exclusion from public facilities resemble?
(c) With which values does the chapter say such laws are inconsistent?
(d) A councillor says: 'The rule is just because the government made it.' Which fact in the chapter shows that being made by a government does not make a law just?
questions.a: (a) The Criminal Tribes Act, 1871. (b) The Jim Crow laws and the apartheid-era laws. (c) The values and principles of justice, and India as a democratic republic. (d) Over 1500 colonial laws made by a government were found discriminatory and repealed, and unjust laws existed in the United States and South Africa.
s: Criminal Tribes Act, 1871
Jim Crow and apartheid laws
Values of justice and a democratic republic
Over 1500 laws repealed; unjust laws elsewhere

questions.q: Compare how India, the United States and South Africa dealt with unjust laws, according to the chapter. (a) Say what India did and name its two examples. (b) Say what the Jim Crow laws did and when they were repealed. (c) Say what the apartheid-era laws did and when they were repealed. (d) State the reason the chapter gives for the repealed Indian laws, and the reason it gives for the American and South African restrictions being unacceptable.
questions.a: (a) India reviewed laws and repealed over 1500 colonial-era laws, for example the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 and the Vernacular Press Act, 1878. (b) Jim Crow laws in parts of the United States prohibited African Americans and other people of colour from using public facilities reserved for white people, including water fountains, public pools and restaurants; they were officially repealed in the 1960s. (c) Apartheid-era laws in South Africa divided people by law on the basis of race, with coloured people facing severe restrictions; they were repealed in 1991. (d) The Indian laws were inconsistent with the values and principles of justice and with India as a democratic republic; the American and South African restrictions kept citizens from public facilities and from a life with dignity.
s: India: over 1500 repealed with two named
Jim Crow: restricted facilities, repealed 1960s
Apartheid: divided by race, repealed 1991
Two reasons: justice and a democratic republic (India); public facilities and a life with dignity (US, South Africa)
Clear comparison across three countries

questions.q: A district court's diary has an empty entry. Fill it with a three or four line imaginary case that meets both aspects of justice. Then label the line that shows each of: a full hearing, the presumption of innocence, and a fair, just and reasonable outcome.
questions.a: Sample: 'Ravi is accused of damaging a neighbour's gate. The court treats him as innocent until the evidence proves otherwise, hears the neighbour and then Ravi with his witnesses, and finally orders him to pay the cost of repair only, as the evidence shows.' Labels: treated as innocent until proved guilty (first line after the accusation); full hearing of both (second); fair and reasonable outcome (last).
s: A full opportunity of hearing shown and labelled
Presumption of innocence shown and labelled
A fair, just and reasonable outcome shown and labelled

questions.q: A student draws India's courts as three separate systems: one for the Centre, one for each State, and one for each district, with none connected to another. Which statement from the chapter corrects the drawing?
questions.a: The judicial system is a unified hierarchy: Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at State level, Subordinate Courts at District level
o: The judicial system is a unified hierarchy: Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at State level, Subordinate Courts at District level
The judicial system is made of Subordinate Courts, with the High Courts and the Supreme Court as optional extras added on top of them
The judicial system has the Supreme Court at the State level and the High Courts at the District level, each with its own separate rules
The judicial system is a hierarchy with the High Courts at the apex and the Supreme Court at the State level of each State in turn

questions.q: Four imaginary persons (illustrative) are considered for the Supreme Court in 2026. Sana: a citizen, a High Court judge since 2021. Tej: a citizen, an advocate of one High Court for ten years. Uma: a citizen, a scholar whom the President of India regards as a distinguished jurist. Vikram: a citizen, an advocate of a High Court for eight years, and nothing more. (a) Say which of the four meet a route in the chapter, and for Sana name the year in which she completes the years her route needs. (b) Say what Vikram lacks and how many more years of practice he would need. (c) Sana turns 61 in 2026. In which year would she retire if she were appointed to the Supreme Court that year, and in which year if she stayed a High Court judge?
questions.a: (a) Sana (High Court judge for five years, completed in 2021 + 5 = 2026), Tej (advocate for ten years) and Uma (distinguished jurist in the President's opinion) meet a route. (b) Vikram has not been a High Court judge, has 8 of the 10 years needed as an advocate, and is not named a jurist; he needs 10 - 8 = 2 more years. (c) A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65: 2026 + (65 - 61) = 2030. A High Court Judge retires at 62: 2026 + (62 - 61) = 2027.
s: Sana, Tej and Uma identified with their routes
Sana's year: 2026
Vikram lacks ten years as an advocate
Two more years
Supreme Court retirement 2030 and High Court retirement 2027

questions.q: Justice Rao (imaginary) was sworn in as a High Court judge in 2019 and has served continuously. She completes the years of service as a High Court judge that the chapter requires for one Supreme Court qualification route in the year ___.

Read the statements about the Supreme Court of India.
1. It is the final interpreter of the Constitution of India.
2. A person can be appointed a Judge only after serving as a High Court judge for five years.
3. A Supreme Court Judge retires on attaining the age of 65 years.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter gives the strength of the Supreme Court as 33+1, which means 33 judges in all, counting the Chief Justice of India among them.' Give the verdict and the correct reading.
questions.a: False. The chapter explains 33+1 as the Chief Justice of India plus 33 Supreme Court judges, so the strength is 34 in all.
s: Verdict: False
Correct reading: CJI plus 33 judges, 34 in all

questions.q: The Supreme Court's strength is 33+1. (a) How many persons does that make in all? (b) A Constitution Bench of five judges (the minimum the chapter gives for advisory cases) is formed from the full strength. How many judges remain for other matters?
questions.a: (a) 33 + 1 = 34. (b) 34 - 5 = 29 judges remain.
s: Part (a): 34
Part (b): 29

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court of India came into existence in 1947, when the country became independent.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court came into existence on the date the Constitution of India came into effect, 26.01.1950.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Two High Courts read the same clause of the Constitution differently, and the matter reaches the apex court. A student asks which court's reading the chapter treats as the last word. Which answer fits?
questions.a: The Supreme Court's, because it is the final interpreter of the Constitution
o: The Supreme Court's, because it is the final interpreter of the Constitution
The older High Court's, because it came into existence before 26.01.1950
The Subordinate Courts', because they are closest to the people
The Chief Justice of India's alone, because he or she heads a High Court as well

questions.q: Rohit says: 'The Supreme Court sits at the apex, so the High Courts and district courts are separate systems that it only watches from outside.' Test the claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls the Indian judicial system a unified system, a hierarchy of courts, with the Supreme Court at the apex level, the High Courts at the State level and Subordinate Courts at the District level. Being at the apex means being the top of that one hierarchy, not outside it.
s: The system is unified, one hierarchy
Three levels in order with the Supreme Court at the apex
Verdict: No, the apex is part of the system

questions.q:
A school quiz sheet (imaginary) has four answers about the Supreme Court.
Answer 1: 'It is seated in New Delhi under Article 124.'
Answer 2: 'A Judge retires at 62.'
Answer 3: 'Judges are appointed by the Governor.'
Answer 4: 'It came into existence on 26.01.1950.'
(a) Which answers are correct?
(b) Correct Answer 2.
(c) Correct Answer 3.
(d) One of the wrong answers would have been right if the words 'Supreme Court' were replaced by 'High Court'. Which one, and what does the chapter say about the appointing authority for that court?
questions.a: (a) Answers 1 and 4. (b) A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65. (c) Every Judge of the Supreme Court is appointed by the President of India. (d) Answer 2, because High Court Judges retire at sixty-two; for a High Court the appointing authority is the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and the Chief Justice of the High Court (so Answer 3 stays wrong).
s: Answers 1 and 4 correct
Retirement at 65
Appointed by the President of India
Answer 2 fits a High Court (62); appointing authority named

questions.q: A stamp shows the Supreme Court's logo with the Sanskrit motto 'yato dharmastato jayah'. A student wants the translation the chapter gives. Which is it?
questions.a: Where there is dharma, there is victory
o: Where there is dharma, there is victory
Equality and dignity for all
Innocent till proved guilty
Where there is law, order

questions.q: A student's note reads: 'The Supreme Court was established by Article 124 and sits in New Delhi. It came into existence on 26.01.1947.' (a) Find the error and correct it. (b) Say what happened on the correct date, as the chapter tells it.
questions.a: (a) The date is wrong: it came into existence on 26.01.1950. (b) That is the date on which the Constitution of India came into effect.
s: Error corrected: 26.01.1950
Date of the Constitution coming into effect

questions.q: A student asks how old the Supreme Court was on 26 January 2026, counting from the day it came into existence, which was the day the Constitution of India came into effect. The answer is ___ years.

Anil says: 'Since the chapter calls the Supreme Court the final interpreter of the Constitution, it must also say that no other court may read the Constitution.' (a) Does the chapter say this? (b) What exactly does the chapter say about the Court's standing in relation to the Constitution?
questions.a: (a) No, the chapter does not say that. (b) It says only that the Supreme Court is the highest court of law in the country and the final interpreter of the Constitution of India.
s: Part (a): the chapter does not say this
Part (b): highest court of law and final interpreter of the Constitution

questions.q: Show that a citizen who has been an advocate of a High Court for nine years, has never been a High Court judge, and is not regarded as a distinguished jurist by the President cannot be appointed to the Supreme Court, by the chapter's qualifications. Go through each route.
questions.a: (i) A Judge of a High Court for five years: she has never been one. (ii) An advocate of a High Court (or more than one) for ten years: she has nine, one short. (iii) A distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President of India: the President does not regard her so. She meets none of the three routes, so she cannot be appointed.
s: Route (i) not met
Route (ii) not met, nine against ten
Route (iii) not met; conclusion

questions.q: Compare the Supreme Court qualification routes (i) and (ii) for a citizen, and say which route is open to a person who has never been a judge or an advocate.
questions.a: Route (i) needs five years as a Judge of a High Court (or High Courts); route (ii) needs ten years as an Advocate of a High Court (or more than one High Court). A person who has been neither can qualify only by route (iii), as a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President of India.
s: Routes (i) and (ii) compared: post and years
Route (iii): distinguished jurist in the President's opinion

questions.q:
A school group visits the Supreme Court and the guide tells them: 'The Court has the Chief Justice and thirty-three other judges, 34 in all. A Judge retires at 62. Since the Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution, every order of every High Court must first be sent to it for approval.'
(a) Which number in the guide's speech does the chapter confirm?
(b) Correct the retirement age for a Supreme Court Judge.
(c) Which sentence has no support in the chapter, and what does the chapter say the Court is?
(d) The guide's retirement age would be right for judges of which court?
questions.a: (a) The strength: the Chief Justice of India plus 33 judges, 33+1 = 34. (b) 65 years. (c) The sentence that every High Court order must first be sent for approval: the chapter says only that the Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution. (d) High Courts, whose Judges retire at sixty-two.
s: Strength of 34 confirmed
Retirement at 65
Approval claim unsupported; final interpreter only
62 belongs to High Court Judges

questions.q: A class compares the Supreme Court with a High Court. Write a comparison with five points: (a) the article that provides for each; (b) the level of the hierarchy at which each sits; (c) who appoints the judges of each; (d) the retirement age of each; (e) what the chapter says about the number of judges in each.
questions.a: (a) Supreme Court: Article 124; High Court: Article 214 (a High Court in each State). (b) The Supreme Court is at the apex; the High Courts are at the State level. (c) Supreme Court Judges are appointed by the President of India; High Court Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court. (d) 65 years for the Supreme Court and 62 years for a High Court. (e) The Supreme Court has 33+1, that is 34; the number of judges in a High Court varies from State to State.
s: Articles 124 and 214
Apex against State level
Appointing authority for each
Retirement ages 65 and 62
33+1 against a number that varies by State

questions.q: Two judges, one of a High Court and one of the Supreme Court, both turn 60 in 2026. By the chapter's retirement ages, which statement is correct?
questions.a: High Court judge in 2028, Supreme Court judge in 2031
o: High Court judge in 2028, Supreme Court judge in 2031
The Supreme Court judge retires in 2028, three years before the High Court judge in 2031
Both retire in 2031, as the chapter gives one retirement age for every court
The High Court judge retires in 2026, three years before the Supreme Court judge in 2029

questions.q: Write one short imaginary profile of a person who meets each of the three qualification routes for a Supreme Court Judge (all being citizens of India), and state in each profile the number of years or the opinion that makes her eligible.
questions.a: Sample: (i) Mala, a citizen who has been a High Court judge for six years. (ii) Naveen, a citizen who has been an advocate of two High Courts for twelve years in all. (iii) Dr Ilango, a citizen and law scholar whom the President of India regards as a distinguished jurist. Each profile fits one route: five years as a High Court judge, ten years as an advocate, or the President's opinion.
s: A profile fitting route (i) with at least five years
A profile fitting route (ii) with at least ten years
A profile fitting route (iii) with the President's opinion

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Public Interest Litigation is itself one of the rights written into Part III of the Constitution, which is why anyone can use it.' Test the claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls PIL an innovation introduced by the Supreme Court to address issues of public concern and to give meaning to the Right to Life under Article 21. It does not say PIL is a right in Part III; Part III holds the Fundamental Rights that writ jurisdiction enforces, and PIL is filed under Articles 32 and 226.
s: PIL is an innovation of the Supreme Court
It gives meaning to Article 21; filed under Articles 32 and 226
Verdict: No, it is not a Part III right

questions.q: Mohan lives in Assam. An officer in his district has violated his Fundamental Rights, and nothing beyond Assam is involved. Priya, a lawyer, finds a rule that affects the Fundamental Rights of people in many States. Which pairing of petitions fits the chapter?
questions.a: Mohan: High Court, Article 226; Priya: Supreme Court, Article 32
o: Mohan: High Court, Article 226; Priya: Supreme Court, Article 32
Mohan directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32; Priya before the High Court under Article 226
Both before the High Court under Article 226, since both live in States of India
Both before the Subordinate Court of their district, under Article 233

questions.q: A student says: 'The first reported PIL proves that the Supreme Court introduced PIL for public concerns, not private grievances.' Evaluate this using the case. (a) What public wrong had Mrs Kapila Hingorani read of? (b) What did her petition seek, and for whom? (c) What did the Court do at once, and what did it do beyond that? (d) Which fact in (b) and (c) shows a public concern rather than one person's grievance? (e) Which right under which article does the chapter say PIL gives meaning to?
questions.a: (a) Under-trial prisoners who had been in jail longer than their punishment would have been if they had been found guilty. (b) The release of all such under-trial prisoners in Bihar. (c) It immediately ordered their release, and issued guidelines to release almost 40,000 under-trial prisoners throughout India. (d) The petition covered a whole group of prisoners and the Court's guidelines reached almost 40,000 throughout India, far beyond one person. (e) The Right to Life under Article 21.
s: The wrong she read of
What the petition sought, and for whom
Release ordered at once; guidelines for almost 40,000
The group and national reach show public concern
Right to Life, Article 21

questions.q: A lawyer read a newspaper report about under-trial prisoners jailed longer than any punishment they could have received. Her writ petition, the first reported PIL, asked for the release of under-trial prisoners in the State of ___.
questions.a: Bihar

questions.q: Rani says: 'Writ petitions are for any quarrel, such as a dispute with a neighbour over a boundary wall.' Which line from the chapter does she overlook?
questions.a: Writ jurisdiction is conferred to enforce Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution
o: Writ jurisdiction is conferred to enforce Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution
Writ jurisdiction is conferred only on the Subordinate Courts of each district for every kind of quarrel
Writ jurisdiction is conferred for enforcing every ordinary law of the legislature in every kind of dispute
Writ jurisdiction lets the executive enforce Part III on the courts' behalf whenever a citizen asks

questions.q: True or False? 'In the first reported PIL, the petitioner was a lawyer who had read about the prisoners in a newspaper, and the Court's guidelines reached prisoners beyond the State named in her petition.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The petition sought release of under-trial prisoners in Bihar, and the Supreme Court also issued guidelines to release almost 40,000 under-trial prisoners throughout India.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Bihar in the petition; almost 40,000 throughout India in the guidelines

questions.q: Ila says: 'A writ petition can be filed only before the Supreme Court.' Jay says: 'A writ petition about a violation of a Fundamental Right within my State can go to the High Court.' (a) Who is right, and under which article? (b) What does the chapter add about when the Supreme Court is approached directly?
questions.a: (a) Jay is right: a citizen may file before the High Court under Article 226 for violation of Fundamental Rights within the territorial limits of the State. Ila is wrong that it is only the Supreme Court. (b) The Supreme Court is approached directly, under Article 32, where the issue has an all India ramification.
s: Part (a): Jay right, High Court under Article 226
Part (b): Supreme Court directly under Article 32 where the issue has an all India ramification

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with what it points to in Column B.
Column A: 1. A villager in one State claims his Fundamental Right was violated within that State.  2. A petition raises an issue with an all India ramification.  3. A lawyer files on a newspaper report to free prisoners jailed longer than any punishment.  4. The Court in 1997 lays down guidelines on harassment at work.
Column B: a. Vishaka & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan  b. Writ petition before the Supreme Court, Article 32  c. Writ petition before the High Court, Article 226  d. The first reported PIL

Assertion (A): Public Interest Litigation gives meaning to the Right to Life under Article 21 of the Constitution.
Reason (R): Public Interest Litigation can be filed only under Article 32.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Residents of a town find that a river polluted by many factories is making thousands of people ill, and no single resident can take up the matter alone. Which feature of the chapter's account of PIL best fits their situation?
questions.a: PIL addresses issues of public concern
o: PIL addresses issues of public concern
PIL is a petition that only a person whose own right is violated may file
PIL is a Fundamental Right listed in Part III of the Constitution
PIL can be started only by the President of India under Article 143

questions.q:
A student tabulates what the Supreme Court did in three PIL cases. Hingorani: ordered the release of under-trial prisoners and issued guidelines to release almost 40,000. M.C. Mehta: took up the cleaning of the River Ganga and the protection of the Taj Mahal. Vishaka: laid down guidelines in 1997. She notices that the chapter mentions a later Act of the Government for only one of the three.
(a) For which case does the chapter mention an Act, and in which year was it enacted?
(b) How many years after the Court's guidelines was that?
(c) What kind of public concern did the M.C. Mehta case take up?
(d) A classmate writes that the Court's guidelines in M.C. Mehta covered almost 40,000 prisoners. Explain the mix-up.
questions.a: (a) Vishaka & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan; the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act was enacted in 2013. (b) 2013 - 1997 = 16 years. (c) Environmental issues: the cleaning of the River Ganga and the protection of the Taj Mahal. (d) The almost 40,000 is the number of under-trial prisoners in the Hingorani case's guidelines; the M.C. Mehta case concerned the environment.
s: Vishaka, with the Act of 2013
16 years
Environmental issues: the Ganga and the Taj Mahal
The 40,000 belongs to the Hingorani case

questions.q: Write one imaginary situation suited to a writ petition before a High Court under Article 226 and one suited to a petition directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32. For each, say what in your situation decides the court.
questions.a: Sample: (1) A villager in one State finds her freedom of speech violated by a local officer; the violation is within the territorial limits of that State, so the High Court under Article 226. (2) A rule that restricts the freedom of religion of people in several States; the issue has an all India ramification, so directly the Supreme Court under Article 32.
s: A situation confined to one State with Article 226
A situation with an all India ramification with Article 32
The deciding feature named for each

questions.q: (a) Name the two environmental matters the Supreme Court took up in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India. (b) Using the chapter's description of what PIL addresses, say why these were suited to PIL.
questions.a: (a) The cleaning of the River Ganga and the protection of the Taj Mahal. (b) PIL is an innovation to address issues of public concern, and these matters concern the public at large, not one private person.
s: Part (a): the Ganga and the Taj Mahal
Part (b): issues of public concern

questions.q:
Read the statements about writs and PIL.
1. A citizen can file a writ petition directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32 where the issue has an all India ramification.
2. PIL is an innovation introduced by the Supreme Court to address issues of public concern, filed under Articles 32 and 226.
3. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India the Supreme Court took up the cleaning of the River Ganga and the protection of the Taj Mahal.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Mrs Hingorani read that some prisoners awaiting trial had been in jail longer than their punishment would have been if found guilty. (a) What did she do? (b) Using the chapter, say why their continued jailing was unjust.
questions.a: (a) She filed a writ petition to secure the release of all such under-trial prisoners in Bihar. (b) They had already been jailed for longer than the punishment they would have received if found guilty, so jailing them further was unjust.
s: Part (a): writ petition for release of under-trial prisoners in Bihar
Part (b): jailed longer than the punishment would have been

questions.q: A student says: 'PIL is a petition that only the person whose rights are violated can file, and it covers only that person.' The first reported PIL case shows which flaw in this?
questions.a: A lawyer who read of the prisoners in a newspaper filed it; the guidelines covered almost 40,000
o: A lawyer who read of the prisoners in a newspaper filed it; the guidelines covered almost 40,000
The Court refused the petition because the lawyer was not herself a prisoner and had only read about the matter in the news
The Court limited its order to the prisoners named by the lawyer in Bihar and to no one else in the country
The petition was filed by the prisoners themselves and was decided in a High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution

questions.q:
Three imaginary petitioners approach the courts in 2026. Rekha, a resident of Assam, says an officer of her district has violated her freedom of speech; nothing beyond Assam is involved. Ajit, a lawyer in Delhi, finds a rule whose effect on Fundamental Rights is felt across India. Sunil has a fence dispute with his neighbour; assume it involves no Fundamental Right.
(a) Where should Rekha file, and under which article?
(b) Where should Ajit file, and under which article?
(c) Does the writ route the chapter describes fit Sunil's fence dispute? Give the reason.
(d) Ajit's friend says he should go to the Delhi High Court because he lives in Delhi. By the chapter's test, why does Article 32 suit his case better?
questions.a: (a) The High Court under Article 226, as the violation is within the territorial limits of the State. (b) Directly the Supreme Court under Article 32. (c) No: writ jurisdiction is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III, and by assumption no Fundamental Right is involved. (d) The chapter's test for Article 32 is that the issue has an all India ramification, not where the petitioner lives; the High Court route is for violations within the State's territorial limits.
s: Rekha: High Court, Article 226
Ajit: Supreme Court, Article 32
Sunil: no Fundamental Right, so writ route not fitted
Test is all India ramification, not residence

questions.q: A student writes: 'Article 32, Article 226 and PIL are three names for the same thing.' Judge this statement. (a) Say what writ jurisdiction enforces. (b) Describe the Article 32 route and its condition. (c) Describe the Article 226 route and its limit. (d) Say what PIL is and under which articles it is filed. (e) Give your verdict on the student's statement.
questions.a: (a) It enforces the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. (b) A citizen files a writ petition directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32 where the issue has an all India ramification. (c) Under Article 226 the petition goes to the High Court and pertains to violations of Fundamental Rights within the territorial limits of the State. (d) PIL is an innovation introduced by the Supreme Court to address issues of public concern and give meaning to the Right to Life under Article 21; it is filed under Articles 32 and 226. (e) The statement is wrong: Articles 32 and 226 are two court routes for writs, and PIL is a development that is filed under both, not a name for them.
s: Writ jurisdiction enforces Part III rights
Article 32 route and condition
Article 226 route and limit
PIL defined and filed under Articles 32 and 226
Verdict: not the same thing, with a reason

questions.q: Distinguish a writ petition under Article 32 from one under Article 226 in terms of the court approached and the reach of the violation. Give a one-line example of your own for each.
questions.a: Article 32: directly before the Supreme Court where the issue has an all India ramification; for example a rule affecting people in many States. Article 226: before the High Court, for violation of Fundamental Rights within the territorial limits of the State; for example an officer's action against a villager in that State only.
s: Article 32: Supreme Court, all India ramification, with an example
Article 226: High Court, within the State, with an example

questions.q: Leela says: 'The chapter names three PIL cases, each about a matter of public concern, and after one of them the Government itself passed an Act.' Test each part against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter names the first reported PIL on under-trial prisoners, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India on the Ganga and the Taj Mahal, and Vishaka & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan on harassment at work, all matters of public concern; and after the Court's 1997 guidelines in Vishaka the Government enacted the 2013 Act.
s: Three cases named with their public concern
Vishaka guidelines of 1997 followed by the Government's Act of 2013
Verdict: Yes, both parts supported

questions.q: Two State governments cannot agree on how to share the water of a river that flows through both. One of them wants the Supreme Court to decide. Under which jurisdiction does the chapter place this?
questions.a: Exclusive original jurisdiction, under Article 131, since the dispute lies between two State governments
o: Exclusive original jurisdiction, under Article 131, since the dispute lies between two State governments
Appellate jurisdiction, after a High Court has certified the case as fit for appeal to the Court at the request of either State
Advisory jurisdiction, because the President must be consulted first on the dispute between the States
Special Leave to Appeal, because no High Court has yet ruled on the dispute between the two States

questions.q: Four imaginary matters reach the Supreme Court in 2026. M1: a State and the Centre disagree on a legal right. M2: the President of India seeks the Court's opinion on a question of law of public importance. M3: a High Court has sentenced a man to death and he appeals. M4: a litigant, with no appeal available, shows that a question of law of general public importance has arisen in a tribunal's order. (a) Name the jurisdiction and article for M1. (b) Name the jurisdiction and article for M2, and the minimum size of the bench. (c) Name the jurisdiction and articles for M3. (d) Name the jurisdiction and article for M4. (e) Which of the four jurisdictions is described as extraordinary and discretionary?
questions.a: (a) Original, exclusive, Article 131. (b) Advisory, Article 143, a Constitution Bench of not less than five judges. (c) Appellate, Articles 134 and 134A. (d) Special Leave to Appeal, Article 136. (e) Special leave, Article 136.
s: M1: original, Article 131
M2: advisory, Article 143, five judges at least
M3: appellate, Articles 134 and 134A
M4: special leave, Article 136
Special leave identified as extraordinary and discretionary

questions.q: A river water dispute between two States goes straight to the Supreme Court under Article ___.

True or False? 'The Supreme Court can hear an appeal from any final order of a High Court under Articles 132, 133 and 134A whether or not the High Court certifies anything.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Under these articles the appeal lies if the High Court itself certifies that the case involves interpretation of the Constitution or a substantial question of law.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the High Court's own certificate is required

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Supreme Court's powers.
1. Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136 is an extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction.
2. Article 144 gives the Court the power to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice.
3. The Court cannot hear appeals from specialised tribunals such as the National Green Tribunal.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Reema says: 'Article 142 lets the Supreme Court pass any order it likes.' (a) Quote the chapter's wording of the power. (b) Which part of the wording limits the kind of order?
questions.a: (a) The Supreme Court has the power to pass any order that is necessary for doing complete justice (Article 142). (b) The order must be necessary for doing complete justice; it is not any order at all.
s: Part (a): any order necessary for doing complete justice
Part (b): the words 'necessary' and 'complete justice' limit it

questions.q: The President of India wants the Supreme Court's view on a question of law of public importance. Which arrangement does the chapter require?
questions.a: A Constitution Bench of not less than five judges hears it under Article 143
o: A Constitution Bench of not less than five judges hears it under Article 143
A single judge hears it under Article 136 and gives a view in chambers
The full Supreme Court of 34 must sit together under Article 131 for it
A High Court hears it first and then certifies it under Article 134A for the Court

questions.q: Farid says: 'The Supreme Court decides disputes between the Centre and a State, and also disputes between two States, but only after a High Court has certified the matter.' Test each part and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: the Court has exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131 over disputes between the Centre and a State and inter-state disputes. The second part is wrong: that is original jurisdiction, so the matter starts in the Supreme Court; High Court certification belongs to the appellate route.
s: First part supported by Article 131
Second part wrong: original, not appellate; no certificate
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
Match each imaginary matter in Column A with the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in Column B.
Column A: 1. A State government and the Centre contest a legal right.  2. A High Court has certified that a final order raises a substantial question of law.  3. The President asks for the Court's opinion on a question of public importance.  4. A litigant with no right of appeal asks the Court's discretion to hear a case from a tribunal, as a question of law of general public importance has arisen.
Column B: a. Advisory jurisdiction  b. Special Leave Petition  c. Original jurisdiction  d. Appellate jurisdiction

A court clerk's note (imaginary) lists three rules about appeals to the Supreme Court.
Rule 1: 'A High Court judgment in a criminal case involving a death sentence can be heard only if the High Court certifies it fit.'
Rule 2: 'From a final order of a High Court, the Supreme Court hears an appeal if the High Court itself certifies that the case involves interpretation of the Constitution or a substantial question of law.'
Rule 3: 'The Supreme Court cannot hear appeals from specialised tribunals.'
(a) Which rule agrees with the chapter?
(b) Correct Rule 1.
(c) Correct Rule 3.
(d) A litigant who lost before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal asks which heading of the chapter lets her go to the Supreme Court. What is it, and which other article might still apply if a question of law of general public importance has arisen?
questions.a: (a) Rule 2. (b) Judgments of the High Court in criminal cases involving a death sentence, or where a judgment is certified as fit for appeal, can be heard (Articles 134 and 134A), so certification is not the only way. (c) The Court has jurisdiction to hear appeals from specialised tribunals. (d) Appellate jurisdiction, as the chapter names the NCLAT; Article 136, Special Leave to Appeal, from any tribunal's order where a question of law of general public importance has arisen.
s: Rule 2 agrees
Rule 1 corrected: death sentence cases need no certificate
Rule 3 corrected: the Court hears appeals from specialised tribunals
Appellate jurisdiction; Article 136 as the other road

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under its advisory jurisdiction, the Supreme Court can give the President of India its opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court is seated in New Delhi.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In a district court, a lawyer cites a legal point that the Supreme Court has already declared. The judge says: 'That is binding only on the High Court of this State.' Which article's wording shows the judge is mistaken?
questions.a: Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India
o: Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India
Article 142: the Court may pass any order necessary for complete justice between the parties
Article 144: civil and judicial authorities shall act in aid of the Supreme Court of India
Article 143: the Court may give its opinion to the President of India on a question of law or fact of public importance

questions.q: A note says: 'Special Leave to Appeal is available only against High Court judgments, and as a matter of right.' Correct the two errors using the chapter.
questions.a: Special Leave to Appeal can be sought from any judgment, decree or order made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India, not only a High Court. It is an extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction, so the Court grants it, not a matter of right.
s: Correction 1: any court or tribunal
Correction 2: discretionary, granted by the Court

questions.q: Show that an inter-state river water dispute cannot be started in a High Court, on the chapter's account. Give three points.
questions.a: (1) The chapter names inter-state disputes such as river water disputes among those over which the Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131. (2) 'Exclusive' means no other court has that jurisdiction, so a High Court cannot take it up at the start. (3) A High Court exercises its powers within its territorial limits, whereas such a dispute is between two States.
s: River water disputes named under Article 131
Exclusive jurisdiction leaves no other court
A High Court acts within one State's territorial limits

questions.q: Compare the Supreme Court's advisory jurisdiction with its appellate jurisdiction on two points: who sets the matter before the Court, and what the Court gives.
questions.a: In advisory jurisdiction the President of India seeks the Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance, and the Court gives its opinion. In appellate jurisdiction a party appeals against a decision of a High Court (certified as the chapter requires, or in a death sentence case) or of a specialised tribunal, and the Court hears the appeal.
s: Advisory: the President seeks; the Court gives an opinion
Appellate: a party appeals from a High Court or tribunal; the Court hears the appeal

questions.q:
In an imaginary matter, the Supreme Court has declared a point of law. An official in a district says the declaration binds only the High Court of that State, and refuses to help carry out the Court's order. The Court is also asked to pass an order that goes beyond one narrow remedy, to do complete justice between the parties.
(a) Which article makes the declared law binding on the district's courts, and on which courts does it bind?
(b) Which article requires the official to act in aid of the Court?
(c) Which article gives the Court the power to pass the wider order?
(d) Predict what the chapter implies for the official's refusal, citing the article wording.
questions.a: (a) Article 141: binding on all courts within the territory of India. (b) Article 144: all civil and judicial authorities shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. (c) Article 142: any order that is necessary for doing complete justice. (d) Under Article 144 the official, a civil authority, must act in aid of the Court, so the refusal is contrary to the chapter; and the law declared binds all courts, not only the State's High Court.
s: Article 141, all courts
Article 144
Article 142
Refusal contrary to Article 144 wording; binding on all courts

questions.q: A question of law of public importance is referred to the Supreme Court by the President of India. The smallest bench the chapter allows for it, a Constitution Bench, has ___ judges.

A newspaper wants one-line headlines for three imaginary matters. Write one headline each for a matter in the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, its advisory jurisdiction and a Special Leave to Appeal, and name the article for each.
questions.a: Sample: (1) Two States contest the sharing of a river's water, Article 131. (2) The President asks for the Court's opinion on a question of law of public importance, Article 143. (3) A litigant seeks leave to appeal against a tribunal's order because a question of law of general public importance has arisen, Article 136.
s: Original jurisdiction situation with Article 131
Advisory jurisdiction situation with Article 143
Special leave situation with Article 136

questions.q: 'The Supreme Court is reached by more than one road.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Name the road for disputes between the Centre and States and between States; give two kinds of appeal it hears; describe the advisory road and Special Leave to Appeal; and say what makes the Court's decisions binding on others.
questions.a: (a) Exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131. (b) Appeals from High Court final orders certified by the High Court itself (Articles 132, 133, 134A), or in criminal cases involving a death sentence or certified fit (Articles 134, 134A), and appeals from specialised tribunals such as the NGT and NCLAT. (c) Under Article 143 the Court gives the President its opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance, heard by a Constitution Bench of not less than five judges. (d) Under Article 136 an extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction to grant special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal where a question of law of general public importance has arisen or to do substantive justice. (e) Article 141: the law declared by the Court binds all courts in the territory of India.
s: Original jurisdiction, Article 131
Two kinds of appeal
Advisory road with the bench size
Special leave described
Article 141 binding force

questions.q: Distinguish the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction from its appellate jurisdiction, and give one example of your own for each.
questions.a: In original jurisdiction a matter starts in the Supreme Court itself, as with a dispute between the Centre and a State under Article 131. In appellate jurisdiction the Court hears an appeal against a lower decision, as with a final High Court order certified by the High Court for a substantial question of law.
s: Original: starts in the Supreme Court, with an example
Appellate: hears an appeal from a lower court or tribunal, with an example

questions.q: Because some States and Union Territories share a High Court, the chapter's count of High Courts falls short of its count of States by ___.
Seema reads that Article 214 provides for a High Court in each State, and then finds only 25 High Courts for 28 States. Which line of the chapter resolves the puzzle?
questions.a: Two or more States or Union Territories may share a common High Court
o: Two or more States or Union Territories may share a common High Court
Some States have been left without a High Court until Parliament makes a law
Each State has a High Court, and the other three belong to the Union Territories alone
Article 214 asks for one High Court for every three States, which gives the 25

questions.q:
A reporter's draft (imaginary) says: 'India has one High Court for every State, 25 of them, and Goa has none because it is too small.'
(a) Name two High Courts from the chapter's table that cover more than one State or Union Territory, with the places each covers.
(b) Which High Court in the table covers two Union Territories and no State?
(c) Correct the reporter's statement about Goa.
(d) Show why 'one High Court for every State' cannot be true given the chapter's own figures.
questions.a: (a) For example the Bombay High Court (Maharashtra, Goa and the Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu) and the Gauhati High Court (Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh); the Calcutta, Kerala, Madras and Punjab & Haryana High Courts also qualify. (b) The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court. (c) Goa is covered by the Bombay High Court, shared with Maharashtra and a Union Territory. (d) The chapter says India has 28 States but 25 High Courts; 28 States cannot each have a separate High Court among only 25, so some High Courts must be shared.
s: Two shared High Courts with their places
Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court
Goa is under the Bombay High Court
28 States against 25 High Courts, so sharing is unavoidable

questions.q:
Read the statements about High Courts.
1. Article 214 provides that every State shall share a common High Court with another State.
2. High Court Judges retire at the age of sixty-two years.
3. Judges of a High Court are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India alone.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: The Kerala High Court covers Kerala and one other place. (a) Name the other kind of unit it covers, and the unit. (b) If the Gauhati High Court's four States each had their own High Court and nothing else changed, how many High Courts would India have in all?
questions.a: (a) A Union Territory, Lakshadweep. (b) 25 - 1 + 4 = 28 High Courts.
s: Part (a): the Union Territory of Lakshadweep
Part (b): 28

questions.q: The Governor of Bihar writes that he alone should pick the next judge of the Patna High Court, since he knows the State best. What does the chapter say about this?
questions.a: The President appoints, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Patna High Court's Chief Justice
o: The President appoints, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Patna High Court's Chief Justice
The Governor appoints High Court judges alone, in consultation with the Chief Minister and the Chief Justice of India, as the head of the State
The Chief Justice of India appoints High Court judges alone, after the Governor of the State has been informed
The President appoints High Court judges alone, without consulting the Governor or any judge of the High Court

questions.q: True or False? 'The Kerala High Court covers Kerala alone, because Article 214 gives every State a High Court of its own.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter's table shows the Kerala High Court covering Kerala and the Union Territory of Lakshadweep, and it says two or more States or Union Territories may share a common High Court.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: it also covers Lakshadweep; High Courts may be shared

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India has 25 High Courts although it has 28 States.
Reason (R): In some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: An imaginary judge was born in 1970 and is a High Court Judge. (a) In which year does she retire, by the chapter's rule? (b) If she were later a Supreme Court Judge instead, in which year would she reach that Court's retirement age?
questions.a: (a) High Court Judges retire at sixty-two: 1970 + 62 = 2032. (b) A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65: 1970 + 65 = 2035.
s: Part (a): 2032
Part (b): 2035

questions.q: In a district, a tribunal passes an order well outside the authority it has. Which power of the High Court does the chapter describe for such a case, and with what caution?
questions.a: Superintendence under Article 227, supervisory in nature and to be exercised sparingly
o: Superintendence under Article 227, supervisory in nature and to be exercised sparingly
Writ jurisdiction under Article 32, to be exercised in every case that comes to its notice
Appointment of the tribunal's members under Article 233, to be used in each year it sits
Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, used only on the President's request

questions.q: Vijay says: 'A High Court uses its writ jurisdiction, hears appeals from subordinate courts and certain tribunals, and supervises subordinate courts, all within its territorial limits.' Test the claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says each High Court exercises its powers within its territorial limits, exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 226, entertains appeals against decisions of subordinate courts in civil and criminal matters and decisions of certain tribunals, and exercises supervisory control over all subordinate courts within its territorial limits.
s: Writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Appeals from subordinate courts and certain tribunals; supervisory control
Verdict: Yes, all within territorial limits
