questions.q: 'The map of the High Courts does not match the map of the States.' Explain this using the chapter. (a) State what Article 214 provides. (b) Give the number of States and of High Courts. (c) Give the reason for the difference. (d) Name a High Court that covers four States and a High Court that covers two Union Territories. (e) Say what the table shows for the Allahabad, Patna and Orissa High Courts.
questions.a: (a) Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court in each State. (b) 28 States and 25 High Courts. (c) In some cases two or more States or Union Territories share a common High Court. (d) The Gauhati High Court covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh; the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court covers the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. (e) Each covers a single State: Allahabad for Uttar Pradesh, Patna for Bihar and Orissa for Odisha.
s: Article 214
28 States, 25 High Courts
Reason: shared High Courts
Gauhati (four States); Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh (two Union Territories)
Allahabad, Patna and Orissa cover one State each

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say a High Court consists of, and about the number of its judges? (b) A reader assumes every High Court has 33 other judges as the Supreme Court does. Why does the chapter's wording not support that?
questions.a: (a) A Chief Justice and other Judges; the number of judges varies from State to State. (b) The 33+1 figure is given only for the Supreme Court; for High Courts the chapter says the number varies, so no single figure applies.
s: Part (a): a Chief Justice and other Judges; number varies by State
Part (b): 33+1 is for the Supreme Court only; High Court numbers vary

questions.q: An imaginary person is appointed a High Court judge at the age of 51 and serves until the retirement age the chapter gives. She serves for ___ years.
Show that the Chief Justice of India alone cannot make an appointment to a High Court, by the chapter's account. Give three points.
questions.a: (1) The chapter says Judges of the High Court are appointed by the President of India, so the appointing authority is the President, not the Chief Justice of India. (2) The President acts in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, which makes him one of those consulted, not the appointing authority. (3) The Governor of the State and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court are also consulted.
s: The President appoints
The Chief Justice of India is consulted
The Governor and the High Court's Chief Justice are also consulted

questions.q:
A newspaper item (imaginary) says: 'Justice Kiran, 59, has been appointed to a High Court by the Governor. A citizen, she was an advocate of two High Courts for eleven years. She will retire at 65.' The year is 2026.
(a) Which two statements in the item does the chapter not support, and what does it say instead?
(b) Does her record meet the qualification in Article 217(2)? Give the reason.
(c) In which year does she retire by the chapter's age?
(d) How many years earlier is that than the retirement the item claims?
questions.a: (a) The Governor appointing her (the President of India appoints, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Chief Justice of the High Court) and retirement at 65 (High Court Judges retire at sixty-two). (b) Yes: she is a citizen and an advocate of more than one High Court for ten years or more, as Article 217(2) requires. (c) 2026 + (62 - 59) = 2029. (d) Retirement at 65 would be 2026 + 6 = 2032, so 3 years earlier.
s: Appointment by the President, not the Governor; retirement at 62, not 65
Qualification met: citizen, advocate for ten years or more
Retirement year 2029
Three years earlier than the claimed 2032

questions.q: A law student's notebook has three blank examples. Fill them: one imaginary situation each for a writ under Article 226, an appeal from a subordinate court, and superintendence under Article 227, labelling the power shown in each.
questions.a: Sample: (1) A villager says an officer violated her Fundamental Right within the State and asks the High Court for a writ, Article 226. (2) A man convicted by a district court appeals to the High Court, an appeal against a subordinate court's decision. (3) The High Court steps in because a tribunal is acting beyond its authority, superintendence under Article 227, used sparingly.
s: Writ situation under Article 226
Appeal from a subordinate court
Superintendence under Article 227

questions.q: Distinguish the High Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 226 from its power of superintendence under Article 227 in what each is about, and say what the chapter says about how sparingly the second is used.
questions.a: Writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights violated within the State's territorial limits. Superintendence under Article 227 is a supervisory power over all courts and tribunals in its territorial jurisdiction, exercised to ensure they act within the bounds of their authority, and it is to be exercised sparingly.
s: Article 226: writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights within the State
Article 227: supervisory power over courts and tribunals, exercised sparingly

questions.q: Four people are considered for a High Court judgeship; assume each is a citizen of India except where stated. Who meets the qualification in Article 217(2)?
questions.a: A person who is a citizen of India and who has held a judicial office in India
o: A person who is a citizen of India and who has held a judicial office in India
A person who has been a legislator for ten years, being a citizen
A person who has been an advocate of a High Court for eight years, being a citizen
A person who is not a citizen of India but who has held a judicial office somewhere in India

questions.q: A newspaper says: 'High Courts only hear appeals. Keeping the lower courts in order is the Supreme Court's job.' Evaluate this against the chapter. (a) Say whether High Courts only hear appeals and name another power. (b) What control does a High Court have over subordinate courts? (c) Name the article and the nature of its power of superintendence. (d) What caution does the chapter attach to it? (e) Say within what limits a High Court exercises all these powers.
questions.a: (a) No: besides entertaining appeals against decisions of subordinate courts and certain tribunals, it exercises writ jurisdiction under Article 226. (b) It exercises supervisory control on the functioning of all subordinate courts within its territorial limits. (c) Article 227: the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction, supervisory in nature, to ensure they act within the bounds of their authority. (d) It is to be exercised sparingly. (e) Within its territorial limits.
s: Not only appeals: writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Supervisory control over subordinate courts
Article 227 superintendence, supervisory
Exercised sparingly
Within its territorial limits

questions.q: A family bought a flat in 2011, paid almost Rs 65 lakh, and found no sign of a building after four years. Their complaint was heard by the National Consumer Commission. Which outcome did the chapter say the Commission ordered?
questions.a: The builder was to return the amount with interest and pay the cost of the litigation
o: The builder was to return the amount with interest and pay the cost of the litigation
The builder was to complete the flats within the next four years at no extra cost
The family was to pay the cost of the litigation and accept a part refund
The builder was to return the amount without interest after a fresh trial

questions.q: A State needs a new District Judge. Under Article 233, the official who appoints her, in consultation with the High Court, is the ___ of the State.
questions.a: Governor

questions.q: Five imaginary disputes (illustrative) are taken to the bodies the chapter's figure lists. For each, name the tribunal, or say that none of the listed tribunals fits. D1: a clerk of a Government office disputes a promotion order. D2: villagers complain that a factory's waste is poisoning their pond. D3: creditors fight over what an insolvent company owes. D4: a retired soldier disputes a service decision of the Armed Forces. D5: two neighbours quarrel over where a fence should stand.
questions.a: D1: Central Administrative Tribunal (service matters of Government employees). D2: National Green Tribunal (environmental issues). D3: National Company Law Tribunal (corporate civil commercial disputes including insolvency and bankruptcy). D4: Armed Forces Tribunal (disputes related to the Armed Forces). D5: none of the six listed tribunals: a fence quarrel between neighbours is not a consumer, service, environmental, corporate, armed forces or electricity dispute.
s: D1: Central Administrative Tribunal
D2: National Green Tribunal
D3: National Company Law Tribunal
D4: Armed Forces Tribunal
D5: none of the listed tribunals, with the reason

questions.q: A trainee says: 'The Constitution does nothing to protect the independence of the judges of the subordinate courts.' Which statement from the chapter answers him?
questions.a: Articles 233 to 237 regulate the organisation of these courts and ensure the subordinate judiciary's independence
o: Articles 233 to 237 regulate the organisation of these courts and ensure the subordinate judiciary's independence
Articles 124 to 128 give the Supreme Court the power to appoint each subordinate judge, so the States have no say in it
Article 214 places the subordinate courts under the same roof as the High Court of each State
Articles 233 to 237 leave the subordinate courts to the legislature of each State to arrange alone

questions.q:
Read the statements about Subordinate Courts and tribunals.
1. Subordinate Courts consist only of District Courts and nothing else.
2. The High Court alone appoints District Judges, without reference to the Governor.
3. Specialised tribunals are quasi-judicial and decide on specific categories of disputes.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter calls only the person who files a case a litigant; the person who gets sued is called a defendant and is not a litigant.' Give the verdict and a correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter defines a litigant as a person involved in a legal case; the person who sues and the person who gets sued are both called litigants.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: both the person who sues and the person who gets sued are litigants

questions.q: Neha says: 'Tribunals are ordinary courts under Articles 233 to 237, and each tribunal can decide every kind of dispute.' Test the claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. Articles 233 to 237 concern the organisation of Subordinate Courts. Tribunals are specialised bodies established under various enactments, quasi-judicial in nature, each deciding specific categories of disputes, such as consumer, service, environmental, corporate, armed forces or electricity disputes.
s: Articles 233 to 237 concern Subordinate Courts
Tribunals established under enactments, quasi-judicial
Verdict: No, each decides specific categories

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Governor of a State appoints District Judges without consulting any other body.
Reason (R): Under Article 233, the Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A visitor writes that Subordinate Courts are 'District Courts and Sessions Courts only'. (a) Name two more kinds the chapter lists. (b) The chapter's list ends with 'etc.'. What does that tell you about the visitor's claim?
questions.a: (a) Revenue Courts and Small Causes Courts. (b) The list is not complete, so the claim that Subordinate Courts are only those two kinds goes beyond the chapter.
s: Part (a): Revenue Courts and Small Causes Courts
Part (b): 'etc.' shows the list is not exhaustive

questions.q: A villager says: 'I will never have anything to do with the courts that matter, because the Supreme Court is far away.' Which statement from the chapter best answers him?
questions.a: It is in the subordinate courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the common people
o: It is in the subordinate courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the common people
The Supreme Court decides every dispute that begins in a village, wherever it started
Subordinate Courts are kept outside the judicial system for the sake of every village
High Courts are organised under Articles 233 to 237, one for each village

questions.q:
A news report (imaginary) on the builder case in the chapter reads: 'After listening only to the family, the National Consumer Commission ordered the builder to pay back the advance of almost Rs 65 lakh, without interest, and left each side to bear its own costs. The names of the parties were withheld because they were minors.'
(a) Find the four places where the report departs from the chapter.
(b) State what the chapter says the Commission ordered.
(c) Why does the chapter say the names were withheld?
(d) Which body does the chapter's figure name for an environmental dispute?
questions.a: (a) The Commission listened to both parties, not only the family; the order included interest; it also ordered the builder to pay the cost of the litigation, not leave each side to bear its own; The names were withheld to protect privacy, not because the parties were minors. (b) To return the amount to the family with interest and to pay the cost of the litigation. (c) To protect their privacy. (d) The National Green Tribunal.
s: Four departures: both parties heard; interest included; cost of litigation ordered; names withheld for privacy, not minority
Order: return with interest and pay the cost of litigation
Names withheld to protect privacy
National Green Tribunal

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why the subordinate judiciary is an important segment of the judicial system.
questions.a: (1) It is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people. (2) The Constitution makes provisions in Articles 233 to 237 to regulate their organisation and to ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary.
s: Close contact with the people
Articles 233 to 237 ensure independence and regulate organisation

questions.q: Ravi says: 'The Governor appoints District Judges alone, and it is for each High Court to maintain the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary.' Test each half and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The second half is right: it is incumbent on each High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary in the concerned States. The first half is wrong: the Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court (Article 233), not alone.
s: Second half supported
First half wrong: consultation with the High Court
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: A body is set up under an Act to settle one particular kind of dispute, and its members decide in a quasi-judicial manner. What does the chapter call such a body?
questions.a: A tribunal, a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes
o: A tribunal, a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes
A Subordinate Court, one of the District Courts organised under Article 233
A Constitution Bench, formed to give the President an opinion
A High Court, set up under Article 214 for one State

questions.q: A customer buys a refrigerator that proves faulty, and the shop refuses a refund. Which body does the chapter's figure name for deciding disputes of this kind?
questions.a: Consumer Fora, which decide consumer disputes
o: Consumer Fora, which decide consumer disputes
The Central Administrative Tribunal, which decides service matters of Government employees
The Green Tribunal for the environment
The Armed Forces Tribunal, which decides disputes related to the Armed Forces

questions.q: A note says: 'Subordinate Courts sit above the High Courts and are free of any control.' Correct the two errors using the chapter.
questions.a: Subordinate Courts are below the High Courts in each State, not above them. They are not free of control: each High Court has supervisory control over all subordinate courts and the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals under Article 227, and it must maintain and uphold their honour and integrity.
s: Correction 1: below the High Courts
Correction 2: High Court's supervisory control and Article 227 superintendence; duty to uphold honour and integrity

questions.q: Write an imaginary dispute for each of three tribunals: the Central Administrative Tribunal, the National Green Tribunal and the Armed Forces Tribunal. Say in one line why each dispute belongs to its tribunal.
questions.a: Sample: (1) A Government clerk disputes a transfer order: service matter of a Government employee, so the Central Administrative Tribunal. (2) Villagers complain that a factory pollutes their pond: an environmental issue, so the National Green Tribunal. (3) A soldier disputes a decision about her service terms: a dispute related to the Armed Forces, so the Armed Forces Tribunal.
s: A service matter for the Central Administrative Tribunal
An environmental dispute for the National Green Tribunal
A dispute related to the Armed Forces with reasons for all three

questions.q: A student says: 'Subordinate Courts matter least, since they sit at the bottom of the hierarchy.' Evaluate this using the chapter. (a) Where do they stand relative to the High Courts? (b) What does the chapter say about the people's contact with them? (c) What do Articles 233 to 237 do for them? (d) What duty does the chapter place on each High Court regarding them? (e) Give your verdict on the student's statement, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) They are a system of courts below the High Courts in each State. (b) It is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people. (c) They regulate the organisation of these courts and ensure the independence of the subordinate judiciary. (d) Each High Court must maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary. (e) The statement is not supported: the chapter calls the subordinate judiciary a very important segment of the judicial system, because it is where the people meet the judiciary.
s: Below the High Courts
Close contact with the people
Articles 233 to 237: organisation and independence
High Court's duty to uphold honour and integrity
Verdict: not supported; a very important segment

questions.q:
In 2026 a State must appoint a District Judge. The High Court, consulted as the chapter requires, recommends one candidate, but the Governor would prefer another.
(a) Who appoints a District Judge, and under which article?
(b) With whom must the appointing authority consult?
(c) Does the chapter say whose view prevails when the Governor and the High Court differ?
(d) Which duty does the chapter place on the High Court towards the judges below it?
questions.a: (a) The Governor of the State, under Article 233. (b) The High Court. (c) No: the chapter says only that the Governor appoints in consultation with the High Court and does not say whose view prevails. (d) It is incumbent on each High Court to maintain and uphold the honour and integrity of the subordinate judiciary.
s: Governor, Article 233
In consultation with the High Court
The chapter does not say whose view prevails
High Court's duty over honour and integrity

questions.q: Distinguish the Subordinate Courts from the tribunals in the chapter by the kinds of matter each handles and by how each is set up.
questions.a: Subordinate Courts broadly include District, Sessions, Revenue and Small Causes Courts, organised under Articles 233 to 237 of the Constitution, and sit below the High Courts in each State. Tribunals are specialised bodies established under various enactments, quasi-judicial in nature, that decide specific categories of disputes.
s: Subordinate Courts: types listed, Articles 233 to 237, below the High Courts
Tribunals: under enactments, quasi-judicial, specific categories

questions.q:
Match each imaginary situation in Column A with the mode of dispute resolution in Column B.
Column A: 1. Two firms refer their quarrel to a retired judge, whose decision binds both of them.  2. A neutral person helps two neighbours reach a settlement but cannot decide the matter for them.  3. A people's forum settles a case pending in a court, without the rigours of formal adjudication.  4. A mobile village-level court hears a dispute using a simplified procedure.
Column B: a. Gram Nyayalayas  b. Lok Adalat  c. Mediation  d. Arbitration

A pamphlet on 'Our modern courts' (imaginary) carries four claims.
Claim 1: 'The Indian Penal Code, 1860 has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.'
Claim 2: 'Litigants can directly check the details of their cases instead of only relying on their lawyers.'
Claim 3: 'Since 2024-2025 a large display screen called the Virtual Justice Clock has stood at the main entrance gates of the Supreme Court.'
Claim 4: 'Gram Nyayalayas are fixed courts at district headquarters.'
(a) Which two claims are wrong?
(b) Correct Claim 1.
(c) Correct Claim 4.
(d) A reader says Claim 2 means litigants no longer need lawyers. Is that what the chapter says? Give its wording.
questions.a: (a) Claims 1 and 4. (b) The Indian Penal Code, 1860 has been replaced by the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita replaces the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. (c) Gram Nyayalayas are mobile, village-level courts that follow a simplified procedure with no technicalities. (d) No: the chapter says litigants can check their case details directly 'instead of only relying on their lawyers', which does not say lawyers are no longer needed.
s: Claims 1 and 4 identified
Claim 1 corrected
